headline: What the gel
trials found.
dek: In the largest testosterone trial, heart events were similar to placebo; clots, fractures and kidney injury were not.

body: [[/testosterone|Testosterone]] is one of the most studied treatments men use, and in recent years it has been tested in large placebo-controlled trials. Approved products are for men whose low levels have a known cause in the testes or the pituitary gland, and labels still say safety and efficacy in men with “age-related hypogonadism”[^androgel] have not been established. This story walks through what those trials found about the heart, bones, prostate and sex drive, and what they could not answer.

The biggest is TRAVERSE. Researchers enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 who reported symptoms of low testosterone, had two fasting levels below 300 ng/dL, and had heart disease or a high risk of it.[^traverse] Each man was randomly assigned, double-blind, to a daily 1.62% testosterone gel, with the dose adjusted to keep levels between 350 and 750 ng/dL, or to a placebo gel.[^traverse] Average treatment lasted 21.7 months, and average follow-up was 33 months.[^traverse] According to the gel’s label, about 61% of patients stopped the gel or placebo during the study.[^androgel] The trial was funded by AbbVie and others.[^traverse]

TRAVERSE was built as a safety test. Its main outcome combined death from heart causes, heart attack and stroke. That outcome occurred in 182 men (7.0%) on testosterone and 190 men (7.3%) on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.96, which met the trial’s preset test for noninferiority.[^traverse] The authors concluded that in these men, testosterone “was noninferior to placebo with respect to the incidence of major adverse cardiac events.”[^traverse] Noninferior means the trial ruled out a large rise in risk; it does not mean the gel lowered risk.

TRAVERSE also recorded higher rates of some other events. The paper reported a “higher incidence of atrial fibrillation, of acute kidney injury, and of pulmonary embolism”[^traverse] in the testosterone group. The label gives the numbers: atrial fibrillation in 3.5% of men on the gel vs 2.4% on placebo, acute kidney injury in 2.3% vs 1.5%, and heart rhythm problems needing treatment in 5.2% vs 3.3%.[^androgel] Blood clots in the veins occurred in 1.7% vs 1.2%, including clots in the lungs in 0.9% vs 0.5%.[^androgel] In TRAVERSE, the gap in systolic blood pressure between groups at 36 months was 1.5 mm Hg.[^androgel]

Then came bones. Because testosterone raises bone density in these men, a TRAVERSE substudy counted fractures, checking each against medical records.[^fracture] After a median of 3.19 years, a fracture had occurred in 91 men (3.50%) on testosterone and 64 men (2.46%) on placebo, a hazard ratio of 1.43.[^fracture] The authors wrote that “testosterone treatment did not result in a lower incidence of clinical fracture than placebo.”[^fracture]

Among men who started with anemia, it corrected in more men on testosterone (45.0% vs 33.9% at 12 months).[^anemia] In men with prediabetes, progression to diabetes did not differ significantly between groups, and the authors wrote that the gel “alone should not be used as a therapeutic intervention to prevent or treat diabetes in men with hypogonadism.”[^diabetes] Mood and energy improved modestly; thinking and sleep quality did not.[^mood] On the prostate, high-grade cancer was found in 5 of 2,596 men on testosterone and 3 of 2,602 on placebo, not a significant difference. Men with a PSA above 3.0 ng/mL were excluded, and PSA rose more with testosterone.[^prostate]

A TRAVERSE substudy on sex drive enrolled 1,161 men who reported low libido: 587 on the gel and 574 on placebo.[^pencina] The main measure was a score of sexual activity, and men on testosterone gained about half a sexual act per day more than men on placebo at 6 and 12 months, an effect still present at 24 months.[^pencina] The authors concluded that the treatment “for 2 years improved sexual activity, hypogonadal symptoms, and sexual desire, but not erectile function.”[^pencina]

The earlier Testosterone Trials, funded by the National Institutes of Health and others, gave 790 men aged 65 or older, with levels below 275 ng/dL, testosterone or placebo gel for one year.[^snyder] Sexual activity, desire and erectile function all rose significantly; the authors described “a moderate benefit with respect to sexual function”[^snyder] but no benefit for vitality or walking distance. In the sexual function arm, 470 men with low libido and a willing partner, testosterone improved 10 of 12 measures of sexual activity; larger rises in testosterone and estradiol tracked with gains in activity and desire, not erectile function.[^cunningham] The main paper noted: “The number of participants was too few to draw conclusions about the risks of testosterone treatment.”[^snyder]

What these trials cannot say is what happens over many years: TRAVERSE treated men for under two years on average. Federal health officials have said as much about the prostate: “important uncertainties remain because prostate cancer can take years to develop and existing studies may not have followed patients long enough to detect long-term effects.”[^hjul] Fertility is another gap. The gel’s label warns that “spermatogenesis may be suppressed through feedback inhibition of pituitary FSH possibly leading to adverse effects on semen parameters including sperm count.”[^androgel] It adds: “Reduced fertility is observed in some men taking testosterone replacement therapy.”[^androgel] With this use or with steroid abuse, it says, “the impact on fertility may be irreversible.”[^androgel]

Regulators have been reacting to this research. On February 28, 2025, FDA told makers to add the TRAVERSE results to all testosterone labels and remove heart-risk language from the boxed warning, while keeping the age-related limitation.[^fda2025] It also required a blood pressure warning after monitoring studies “confirmed an increase in blood pressure with use of all testosterone products, class-wide.”[^fda2025] FDA held an expert panel on testosterone for men on December 10, 2025.[^panel] On June 18, 2026, HHS proposed three label changes: removing the age-related limitation, narrowing the prostate cancer contraindication to men with metastatic disease, and dropping a warning about enlarged-prostate symptoms.[^hjul]

Those are proposals, and the research behind them still has the limits its authors described: men at high heart risk, about two years of treatment, and several side effects that ran higher on the gel than on placebo.
